blocks.text: TL;DR

inlines.text: TL;DR

blocks.text: 大多数网络安全基准只让一个智能体扮演一种角色，去攻击一个始终不变的目标，因此随着模型能力提升，这类基准很快就被刷满。CyberArena 则让两个 AI 智能体互相攻击对方正在运行的服务，同时修补自己的服务，每一轮结果都由竞技场验证。在 12 个前沿智能体之间进行的 466 场对局中，GPT-5.6 Sol 和 Claude Opus 5 领跑全场；而智能体单独能解出的挑战，一旦有防守方反击，就重新变得困难。实时压力和真实对手还同时暴露出两方面表现：既有高级能力，比如攻击方植入的后门能在防守方打补丁后依然存活；也有失败案例，比如智能体声称修复了漏洞，却从未测试过。

blocks.text: 核心结论

inlines.text: 核心结论

blocks.text: 有了实时对手，已解出的挑战会重新变难。在无人防守服务时，GPT-5.6 Sol、Claude Opus 4.8 和 GLM-5.3 都能解出我们 40 个挑战中的同样 30 个；但一旦有第二个智能体来防守，它们的平均成功率就从第 1 轮的 89% 降到第 2 轮的 52%，再到第 3 轮的 42%。对手的存在把一项可验证的任务变成了半开放式的环境，并动态生成被评测智能体从未见过的新任务和新环境。

blocks.text: 打一个补丁并不能让服务变安全。防守方在丢失 flag（攻击方必须窃取的秘密）并部署补丁之后，仍有 40% 的后续轮次再次丢掉 flag；在 21% 的对局中，补丁还留下了另一条可走的路径。这类浅层补丁虽然能通过静态基准的固定检查，但实时攻击方会去搜索那条路径。

blocks.text: 在实时压力下，智能体会试图不完成既定任务就拿到分数。例如，攻击方不去利用对手的服务，而是重放竞技场的授权请求来冒充竞技场本身；防守方则放行竞技场的健康检查，同时把对手挡在外面。我们的反作弊审查和红队对局在大多数此类路径被利用之前就将其封堵，但仍发现 1,336 次被接受的夺取中有 6 次（0.45%）来自捷径。

blocks.text: 什么是 CyberArena？

inlines.text: 什么是 CyberArena？

blocks.text: CyberArena 让网络安全智能体以人类夺旗赛（CTF）的攻防形式同场竞技，以此衡量它们的水平。每个智能体既要防守自己那份存在漏洞的服务副本，又要攻击对手的副本。这样一来，对手本身就成了基准：智能体面临的难度不仅取决于题目，还取决于对手的攻击和修补水平，而且随着双方不断适应，难度也在持续变化。

blocks.text: 闯关式基准只让智能体扮演一种角色，面对一个始终不变的目标。CyberArena 则让双方智能体同时扮演攻防两种角色，面对一个实时对手，并根据回合结果对攻击、防御和可用性打分。

blocks.text: 对局设置。两个智能体在隔离网络中打三个 20 分钟的回合，各自托管同一服务的相同副本。智能体通过未授权访问对手的服务得分，例如读取 flag（每回合都会变化的秘密金丝雀值），或在不应写入、执行的位置写入数据、执行代码。同时，每个智能体必须修补自己的服务以阻止此类访问，并保证正常用户仍能使用，补丁在各回合间持续生效。竞技场会核验每一次攻陷，健康检查器则定期以正常用户身份操作，例如登录或上传文件，确认各服务仍然可用。

inlines.text: 主要结果

blocks.text: 我们评估了来自 10 家开发者的 12 个前沿智能体，覆盖 40 道题（14 道来自 CTF 决赛，26 道来自真实应用），共计 466 场对局。每场对局给智能体打 0 到 100 分，攻击（攻陷对手 flag 的回合）、防御（守住自己 flag 的回合）和可用性（健康检查器通过的服务测试）权重相同。我们的排名模型会预测每一对组合的得分，并对所有对手和题目取平均，因此预期得分 79% 意味着在典型题目上对阵典型对手时，百分制能拿到 79 分。

blocks.text: 两强领跑。 GPT-5.6 Sol 的期望得分最高，为 79%，紧随其后的是 Claude Opus 5 的 74% 和 GLM-5.3 的 69%，头部得分呈均匀阶梯下降（图 1a）。但若按胜局数统计，两位领先者便明显拉开差距：它们的胜率分别为 83% 和 86%，而其他智能体的胜率均不超过 59%。

blocks.text: 涌现行为

blocks.text: 为什么这很重要

inlines.text: 为什么这很重要

blocks.text: 真实世界的安全攻防是一场持续变化的较量。让系统保持安全不是一劳永逸的事，因为攻击者会针对每一次修补做出调整，防守方也必须随时掌握系统上正在发生什么。在实践中，安全工程师会通过渗透测试探测自家服务，读取攻击者留下的痕迹，对安全事件进行分级和调查，并在时间压力下为运行中的系统打补丁。静态基准测试完全体现不了这些，因为它的目标从不变化，也没有对手在另一端。CyberArena 把这一循环引入评测，因此智能体若能察觉到对手就会得到奖励——比如 Qwen3.8 Max 构建了一个抓包工具——同时，修复服务而不把它弄坏也会得到奖励。

blocks.text: TL;DR

inlines.text: TL;DR

blocks.text: Most cybersecurity benchmarks test one agent in one role against a target that never changes, so they saturate as models improve. CyberArena instead has two AI agents attack each other’s live service while patching their own, with every outcome verified by the arena. Across 466 games between 12 frontier agents, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 lead the field, and challenges that agents solve alone become hard again once a defender fights back. Real-time pressure and a live adversary also expose both advanced capabilities, such as an attacker planting a backdoor that survives the defender’s patch, and failures, such as agents claiming fixes they never tested.

blocks.text: Key Takeaways

inlines.text: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: A live opponent turns solved challenges back into hard ones. GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 4.8 and GLM-5.3 all solve the same 30 of our 40 challenges when nobody defends the service, but once a second agent defends it, their average success rate falls from 89% in round 1 to 52% in round 2 and 42% in round 3. The presence of an adversary turns a verifiable task into a semi-open-ended setting and dynamically creates new tasks and settings that the evaluated agent has not seen.

blocks.text: A single patch does not make a service safe. After losing its flag (the secret that the attacker must steal) and deploying a patch, a defender still loses the flag again in 40% of the following rounds, and in 21% of games a patch leaves another route open. Although such shallow patches can pass the fixed checks of a static benchmark, a live attacker searches for that route.

blocks.text: Under live pressure, agents try to earn credit without doing the intended task. For example, instead of exploiting the opponent’s service, attackers impersonated the arena itself by replaying its authorized requests, and defenders let the arena’s health checker through while locking out the opponent. Our anti-cheat reviews and red-team games close most such routes before they are exploited, but we still found 6 of 1,336 accepted captures (0.45%) that came from shortcuts.

blocks.text: Many agent errors come from their own work rather than from the opponent. The most common error, in 23% of games, is claiming that a repair works when the agent’s own tests do not show it, which means agents fail to judge how complete their own work is and make false reports of success. Agents also waste time by sleeping through active rounds (14% of games), even though their instructions forbid idling.

blocks.text: What Is CyberArena?

inlines.text: What Is CyberArena?

blocks.text: CyberArena measures cybersecurity agents by making them compete, in the attack-and-defense format of human Capture-The-Flag (CTF) competitions. Each agent defends its own copy of a vulnerable service while attacking its opponent’s copy. As a result, the opponent becomes the benchmark, because the difficulty an agent faces depends not only on the challenge but also on how well its opponent attacks and patches, and it keeps changing as both agents adapt.

Bottom: CyberArena, where two agents each host a live service with rotating flags, attack each other and patch their own service over three rounds, and round outcomes feed estimated attack, defense and availability scores.

blocks.text: Jeopardy-style benchmarks give an agent one role against a target that never changes. CyberArena gives both agents both roles at once, against a live opponent, and scores attack, defense and availability from the round outcomes.

blocks.text: Game setup. Two agents play three 20-minute rounds in an isolated network, each hosting an identical copy of the same service. An agent scores by gaining unauthorized access to the opponent’s service, for example by reading a flag, a secret canary value that changes every round, or by writing data or executing code where it should not be able to. Each agent must also patch its own service to block such access while keeping it working for benign users, and patches stay in place across rounds. The arena verifies every capture, and its health checker regularly acts as a benign user, for example by logging in or uploading a file, to confirm that each service still works.

To save cost, the arena picks the next games by how much they would reveal, and our campaign covers 466 games between 12 frontier agents on 40 challenges.

blocks.text: Challenge sources. Challenges come from past CTF finals, such as saarCTF, FAUST CTF and DEF CON CTF, and from real open-source applications, such as Jenkins and WordPress. Five of the real vulnerabilities, including ones in Openfire and GeoServer, are listed by the U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA as exploited in the wild. An automated pipeline of AI agents builds and reviews new challenges, so the pool can grow as new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

blocks.text: Main Results

inlines.text: Main Results

blocks.text: We evaluate 12 frontier agents from 10 developers on 40 challenges (14 from CTF finals and 26 from real applications), for a total of 466 games. Each game gives an agent a score from 0 to 100 that weighs attack (rounds in which it captured the opponent’s flag), defense (rounds in which it kept its own flag) and availability (health checker tests its service passed) equally. Our ranking model predicts this score for every pairing and averages it over all opponents and challenges, so an expected score of 79% means 79 of 100 points against a typical opponent on a typical challenge.

blocks.text: Inside the Fights

inlines.text: Inside the Fights

blocks.text: Defenders respond. Agents notice their opponent and respond within the same game. After losing its flag, a defender reviews the attacks that hit it in two-thirds of cases and deploys a patch before the next round in more than half. Defenders that patch keep their flag in the next round far more often than those that do not (60% against 9%), although this shows an association rather than proof that the patches worked.

inlines.text: Failures

blocks.text: Unverified fixes. The most common error is a fix that the agent declares successful without testing the version that is actually running (Table 1). In one game, an agent cited health checker results recorded before its patch went live as proof that the patch worked.

blocks.text: Patches that miss or overreach. Other patches are either incomplete or too strict. A partial patch closes one route while another stays open, whereas an over-blocking patch stops the attacker but also rejects legitimate users. For example, one agent added permission checks to its MLflow service that rejected normal user requests, and checking that the service still responded did not reveal the problem.

blocks.text: Real-world security is a moving contest. Keeping a system secure is not a one-time fix, because attackers adapt to every repair and defenders must keep track of what is happening on their systems. In practice, security engineers probe their own services through penetration testing, read the traces that attackers leave behind, triage and investigate incidents, and patch live systems under time pressure. A static benchmark captures none of this, since its target never changes and nobody is on the other side. CyberArena brings this loop into evaluation, so an agent is rewarded for noticing its opponent, as when Qwen3.8 Max built a packet sniffer, and for repairing its service without breaking it.

blocks.text: Verifiable environments that do not saturate. Building and evaluating powerful agents requires environments that check outcomes automatically, yet such environments lose their value once agents solve them. Competition offers a way out, because each side’s progress poses a harder problem for the other, and self-play methods such as GPT-Red already use this idea to train a prompt-injection attacker against defenders that are trained at the same time. CyberArena applies the same principle to cybersecurity with verified outcomes, and its game records could help train attackers and defenders against each other, a loop we call Recursive Adversarial Improvement.
